pp-1.howToGetThere: Historic centre of La Orotava, near the Plaza de la Constitución
pp-1.recommendations: Visit during the day. Look at the columns by the altar and search for the gargoyles at the back of the church.
pp-1.fullHistory: The Church of La Concepción is one of the most enigmatic temples in the Canary Islands. Its location was chosen on telluric criteria, taking advantage of the natural energy lines of the terrain. The architects incorporated Masonic and Hermetic symbolism into its design, visible in the columns with inverted triangles that represent esoteric concepts. The gargoyles at the back are especially curious, as they depict exhibitionist figures similar to ancient Celtic fertility idols, something very unusual in a Catholic church.

pp-2.recommendations: Respect private property. It can be viewed from the outside.
pp-2.fullHistory: La Orotava's connection with the tragedy of Catalina Lercaro is less well known than the main house in La Laguna, but just as unsettling. After the suicide of Catalina, who threw herself into a well before her forced wedding, the Lercaro family left their residence in La Laguna and settled in the La Orotava Valley. Some believe they were trying to flee Catalina's ghost, others that they were simply escaping social shame. Local legends suggest that Catalina's spirit followed the family.

pp-3.howToGetThere: Centre of La Orotava, emblematic historic building
pp-3.recommendations: Visit during cultural events. Ask long-serving staff about the stories.
pp-3.fullHistory: The Liceo de Taoro is an important cultural centre in La Orotava with over a century of history. Over the years, staff and visitors have reported unexplained experiences in the building, especially at night. Paranormal investigations have documented these phenomena, although some reserve is kept so as not to affect the centre's cultural activities.

pp-4.recommendations: Attend cultural events. Staff may share their experiences.
pp-4.fullHistory: The Teobaldo Power Auditorium, despite being a relatively modern building, has accumulated reports of unexplained phenomena. The testimonies come mainly from technical staff and artists rehearsing at night. Noises with no apparent source are described, especially in the dressing rooms and technical areas.

pp-5.howToGetThere: Old town of La Orotava, near San Francisco street
pp-5.recommendations: Visit at dusk. Ask elderly residents of the area.
pp-5.fullHistory: The Green Shadow is one of the most persistent urban legends of La Orotava. For generations, neighbours have reported seeing a greenish figure in Placita Rosales, especially when the sun goes down. The origin of this apparition is unknown, although some link it to old stories of the neighbourhood.

pp-6.recommendations: Visit in a group and with a guide. The area is poorly lit at night.
pp-6.fullHistory: The Cross of the Hanged marks a place of sad memory in La Orotava. For centuries, this was the spot where death sentences by hanging were carried out. According to tradition, the souls of the condemned remain bound to this place, manifesting especially at night.

pp-7.howToGetThere: From the historic centre of La Orotava
pp-7.recommendations: Go with a local guide. Wear footwear suitable for a ravine.
pp-7.fullHistory: The Barranco de Araujo is known in La Orotava for a tragedy of the past whose specific details have blurred over time. Local mystery tours include this spot on their routes, recounting the story of the tragic death that marked the place.

pp-8.activityHours: All day - Most intense at night

pp-8.howToGetThere: San Francisco street, historic centre of La Orotava. An emblematic, easily recognisable building.
pp-8.recommendations: Open to the public as a museum. It can be visited during business hours. Pay attention to the sensations in the rooms on the upper floor.
pp-8.fullHistory: The Casa de los Balcones is one of the most emblematic buildings in La Orotava and an important tourist attraction. This 17th-century mansion currently houses a museum of Canarian crafts. However, beneath its architectural beauty lies a darker story. According to local tradition, the building was constructed on land that was formerly a cemetery. For years, visitors and staff have reported ghostly figures appearing in different parts of the house, as well as a constant feeling of being watched by invisible presences. Some witnesses describe sudden changes in temperature and a particularly heavy atmosphere in certain rooms.

pp-9.howToGetThere: San Agustín street, 22, historic centre of San Cristóbal de La Laguna
pp-9.recommendations: Visit during museum hours (Mon–Sat 9:00–19:00, Sundays and public holidays 10:00–17:00). Ask about the legend on the guided tour.
pp-9.fullHistory: The legend places Catalina Lercaro in this palace: forced to marry against her will, she is said to have taken her own life by throwing herself into a well in the courtyard on her wedding day. As it was a suicide, the Church refused to give her a Christian burial, so tradition holds that her body was buried in one of the rooms of the house. An investigation by the museum's managers into the parish burial registers found no documentary evidence that a young Catalina had died in the palace, so it is now considered an urban legend with no confirmed historical basis, although it remains the most frequently cited one in La Laguna.

pp-10.howToGetThere: Plaza del Adelantado, historic centre of San Cristóbal de La Laguna
pp-10.recommendations: Check the convent visiting hours; it is still inhabited by cloistered nuns.
pp-10.fullHistory: Founded in 1600 by Juan de Cabrejas and María de Salas on the former houses of the adelantado Alonso Fernández de Lugo, the convent opened in 1611 with four nuns from Seville and came to house around a hundred. Its present fame comes from the incorrupt body of the nun María de Jesús de León y Delgado, who died in 1731 and was exhumed three years later at the request of Amaro Rodríguez Felipe, who paid for a wooden coffin for her, something unusual since nuns were buried directly in the earth. The discovery of the undecomposed body fed her reputation for popular sanctity.

pp-11.howToGetThere: Obispo Rey Redondo street, historic centre of San Cristóbal de La Laguna
pp-11.recommendations: Attend a performance and ask the technical staff about their experiences.
pp-11.fullHistory: Built in 1915 to plans by the architect Antonio Pintor and reopened after a restoration in 2008, the Teatro Leal is one of the most active historic stages in La Laguna. The city's paranormal-themed guided tours cite it alongside the Lercaro Palace as a place where staff have reported unexplained phenomena, although unlike the latter there is no specific legend attached, only scattered accounts from workers and artists.

pp-12.howToGetThere: Historic centre of San Cristóbal de La Laguna, near the Lomo de la Concepción
pp-12.recommendations: A good contrast with the rest of the route: here the mystery has a known solution.
pp-12.fullHistory: On the night of 2 November 1865, the night watchmen of La Laguna began reporting a ghost by the fountain in the Plaza del Juego de los Bolos: a figure wrapped in sheets that dragged chains and vanished down the Callejón del Osario. The legend, very popular for months, was eventually solved: behind the sheet was a well-off young man named Gallardo who exploited the neighbours' superstition and the watchmen's fear to meet his sweetheart in secret, using the ghost costume to clear the square without raising suspicion. It is one of the few paranormal legends in La Laguna with a documented, non-supernatural ending.

pp-13.howToGetThere: Plaza Isla de La Madera, s/n, 38003 Santa Cruz de Tenerife
pp-13.recommendations: Attend a performance and ask the technical staff about their experiences backstage.
pp-13.fullHistory: The Teatro Guimerá, inaugurated on 25 July 1851, is the oldest theatre in the Canary Islands and remains active as a venue with a regular programme. The legend most often repeated by technical staff and the city's night tours tells of a jilted woman who is said to have died during a performance and whose spirit continues to haunt the building, especially the boxes and the space behind the stage, on nights with no show.

pp-14.howToGetThere: Between Méndez Núñez and Pilar streets, centre of Santa Cruz de Tenerife
pp-14.recommendations: Walk through the park at nightfall, when the apparition is said to appear according to the legend.
pp-14.fullHistory: The García Sanabria Park, the green heart of Santa Cruz de Tenerife since its remodelling in the 1920s, is described by local mystery routes as a place that 'turns into another at night': a magical and gloomy space where the legend of the 'woman with the veil' is told, a female presence that appears among the paths and ponds after dark. To this is added the esoteric reading of part of its statuary, with symbolism that some guides link to secret societies, and scattered testimonies of strange phenomena in homes next to the park.

pp-15.howToGetThere: Plaza del Príncipe, historic centre of Santa Cruz de Tenerife, next to Villalba Hervás street
pp-15.recommendations: Visit at nightfall; combine with the rest of the 'Santa Cruz Tenebrosa' route.
pp-15.fullHistory: Built in 1855 on the former orchard of the San Francisco convent and named to coincide with the birth of Alfonso XII, the Plaza del Príncipe is one of the most photographed corners of Santa Cruz thanks to its centuries-old Indian laurel trees. The city's mystery routes include it in their tours, citing spectral apparitions in the square itself and unexplained events linked to a historic house in the area, although there is no single established legend as at other points on the route.

pp-16.howToGetThere: Access via the A-222 from Zaragoza, about 45 km to the south.
pp-16.recommendations: Do not enter outside the authorised guided tours because of the risk of the structures collapsing.
pp-16.fullHistory: During the summer of 1937, Belchite was the scene of one of the bloodiest battles of the Spanish Civil War, leaving thousands dead in its streets. Franco ordered that the old town not be rebuilt and that a new one be built alongside it. Since the 1980s, researchers from around the world have recorded in its ruins some of the clearest psychophonies in the history of parapsychology.

pp-17.howToGetThere: Campanillas district, next to the A-357 motorway on the outskirts of Málaga.
pp-17.recommendations: Do not cross the perimeter, as it is private property and partly in ruins.
pp-17.fullHistory: Built in the mid-19th century by the wealthy Heredia family, Cortijo Jurado has 365 windows (one for every day of the year) and a Gothic chapel. The dark legend arose with the disappearance of several young women between the late 19th and early 20th centuries, popularly attributed to rituals of the local elites.

pp-18.howToGetThere: On the outskirts of the town of Aigües (Alicante), on the slopes of the Sierra del Cabeçó d'Or.
pp-18.recommendations: Extreme caution; collapsed ceilings and floors inside.
pp-18.fullHistory: Opened in 1838 as the Hotel Balneario Miramar thanks to its curative thermal waters, the Marquis of Bosch promoted a luxury complex. In 1936 it was acquired by the State to treat children with tuberculosis. After being abandoned in the late 1960s, the building became one of the favourite places of paranormal researchers on the Mediterranean coast.

pp-19.howToGetThere: From Vitoria towards the Treviño enclave, taking the country road from Imiruri.
pp-19.recommendations: Wear mountain footwear and respect the heritage setting.
pp-19.fullHistory: Ochate, whose original name means 'Wolf's Gate', was left uninhabited after the third epidemic of 1864. Only the tower of the church of San Miguel and the nearby hermitage of Burgondo remain standing. In the 1980s the photographer Prudencio Muguruza captured a famous image of a white sphere flying over the site, putting Ochate on the international ufological map.

pp-20.howToGetThere: Plaza de Cibeles 2, Madrid. Banco de España metro (Line 2).
pp-20.recommendations: Attend the official dramatised guided tours organised by Casa de América.
pp-20.fullHistory: José de Murga y Reolid, 1st Marquis of Linares, married Raimunda de Osorio, later discovering that they were half-siblings on their father's side. According to the legend, they had a daughter nicknamed Raimundita to conceal the incest, who was supposedly murdered and buried in the palace walls. Although modern historians question the physical existence of the girl, testimonies from guards and visitors persist to the present day.

pp-21.recommendations: The current complex houses private film studios; do not enter closed areas without authorisation.
pp-21.fullHistory: Located in a leafy pine wood to take advantage of the pure air, it housed terminally ill patients with tuberculosis and lung cancer. Patients frequently threw themselves from the 9th floor into the inner garden nicknamed 'the jungle'. Numerous horror films have been shot there because of its charged atmosphere.

pp-22.recommendations: Take care on days of thick fog; always stay on the marked trails.
pp-22.fullHistory: La Mussara was abandoned in 1959 after a prolonged drought. The church of San Salvador and the ruins of the farmhouses emerge from a fog that often covers the plateau suddenly. In 1991, a hiker disappeared during a walk in broad daylight, leaving his car locked with all his belongings in the village, a case that shocked Catalonia.

pp-23.howToGetThere: Baztán Valley, 400 metres from the town centre of Zugarramurdi along a signposted path.
pp-23.recommendations: Also visit the Witches Museum in the village before walking through the cave.
pp-23.fullHistory: The caves contain no cave paintings or notable prehistoric remains, but they are the epicentre of witchcraft in Spain. In 1610, the inquisitor Valle-Alvarado prosecuted more than 30 villagers accused of worshipping the he-goat (Akerbeltz) in this natural cavity. Eleven people perished burned at the stake in Logroño.

pp-24.howToGetThere: Calle Real 5, Bélmez de la Moraleda, Sierra Mágina region (Jaén).
pp-24.recommendations: Visit the Faces Interpretation Centre in the former school building.
pp-24.fullHistory: On 23 August 1971, María Gómez Cámara first noticed a stain in the shape of a human face in her kitchen. Although her husband broke up the floor with a hoe and poured new concrete, the face reappeared days later with greater clarity. Chemical analyses, notarial seals and geological surveys have debated for more than 50 years between chemical fraud and the most important genuine paranormal phenomenon in Europe.

pp-25.recommendations: The monumental complex can be visited without staying overnight, including the collegiate church and the Minyona Tower.
pp-25.fullHistory: Medieval legend has it that the young Christian Adalés fell in love with a Muslim prince at court. Her father and brothers punished her by shutting her away for life in the Minyona Tower, where she died of grief. Both cleaners and guests who spent the night in room 712 have for years reported anguished dreams and the noise of furniture being dragged overhead when the floor was completely empty.

pp-26.howToGetThere: From Alfacar, going up towards the Alfaguara Camp along the forest track.
pp-26.recommendations: Ideal for daytime hiking; do not go in at night without powerful torches.
pp-26.fullHistory: Berta Wilhelmi founded this sanatorium in 1923 in the middle of nature to offer heliotherapy treatment to tuberculosis patients from humble families. During the Civil War the sanatorium fell into disuse and was finally abandoned in the post-war period. Today only a few walls remain, covered by pines that give the spot a romantic and mysterious look.

pp-27.accessibility: Valley surroundings accessible; building with bricked-up entrances

pp-27.howToGetThere: From Navacerrada, take the turn-off towards the Barranca Valley.
pp-27.recommendations: Enjoy the natural surroundings of La Barranca; do not try to force entry into the closed building.
pp-27.fullHistory: Located in the beautiful Barranca valley, surrounded by pine forests at 1,400 metres above sea level, the centre closed its doors in the 1990s after the transfer of health responsibilities. Despite having been bricked up on several occasions, its imposing stone silhouette and slate roofs continue to attract enthusiasts of strange phenomena.

pp-28.accessibility: Observation from high viewpoints on La Palma, Tenerife and El Hierro
phenomena: Clear appearance of a mountainous landmass with valleys

pp-28.howToGetThere: Visible on clear days to the west from viewpoints on La Palma (El Paso, Fuencaliente) and Tenerife (Icod, Los Realejos).
pp-28.recommendations: Look at the horizon at sunset, when the sun outlines the sea haze.
pp-28.fullHistory: Inspired by the voyage of the Irish monk Saint Brendan of Clonfert in the 6th century, the island was sighted by navigators and sailors for centuries. Royal expeditions set out from the Canary Islands in the 16th and 18th centuries to take possession of it in the name of the Crown of Spain. The famous photo taken in 1958 by Manuel Rodríguez Quintero from Los Realejos revived the enigma.

pp-29.accessibility: Visible when the reservoir level drops below 30%

phenomena: Ancestral solar astronomical alignment at the solstice

pp-29.howToGetThere: North shore of the Valdecañas reservoir, municipality of El Gordo (Cáceres).
pp-29.recommendations: Scrupulously respect the megaliths; do not touch or move the stones.
pp-29.fullHistory: Excavated in the 1920s by the German archaeologist Hugo Obermaier, the Guadalperal dolmen has a ring of 140 stones up to two metres high and an entrance corridor. In 1963 the construction of the Tagus dam submerged it. In 2019, a historic drought exposed it for the first time in 50 years, astonishing the international archaeological community.

pp-30.accessibility: Ruins in open country - Beware of wells and holes

pp-30.howToGetThere: Country road from Carmona towards the Seville countryside.
pp-30.recommendations: Preferably visit in daylight because of collapses in the floor.
pp-30.fullHistory: Founded in the 15th century on an isolated estate, the monastery enjoyed centuries of splendour before being abandoned with the confiscations of the 19th century. Popular legend says that one stormy night the monks were found dead in the refectory with expressions of horror, giving rise to the nickname 'Monastery of the Devil'. In recent decades it has been frequented by mystery enthusiasts.
